rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: Distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors. Although in an extrinsic semiconductor \(n_e \neq n_h\), yet it is electrically neutral. Why ?
rows.solution:
**Intrinsic against extrinsic.**

| | Intrinsic semiconductor | Extrinsic semiconductor |
|---|---|---|
| Composition | Pure — germanium or silicon with no deliberate impurity | Doped with a trivalent or pentavalent impurity, roughly 1 atom in \(10^{6}\) |
| Carrier counts | \(n_e = n_h = n_i\) | \(n_e \neq n_h\); one type dominates |
| Source of carriers | Thermal breaking of covalent bonds only | Mostly the dopant, which needs almost no energy to ionise |
| Conductivity | Very low, and zero at absolute zero | Far higher, and controllable through the doping level |
| Dependence on temperature | Rises steeply with \(T\) | Almost flat over the working range, because the dopant is already fully ionised |
| Types | Only one | **n-type** (pentavalent dopant, electrons in majority) and **p-type** (trivalent dopant, holes in majority) |

**Why it stays electrically neutral even though \(n_e \neq n_h\).**

The question invites a wrong answer, so it is worth being exact about what \(n_e\) and \(n_h\) count: they count only the **mobile** carriers. Neutrality is a statement about *all* the charge present, fixed charge included.

Take n-type silicon. Each pentavalent donor atom — arsenic, say — uses four of its five valence electrons in covalent bonds and gives up the fifth to the conduction band. That electron is now mobile and counts in \(n_e\).

But the atom it left is still there, locked in the lattice, and it is now a **positively charged donor ion**. Its charge is exactly \(+e\), equal and opposite to the electron it released.

So every extra electron in \(n_e\) is matched, one for one, by an immobile positive ion. Add them up:

total negative charge (mobile electrons) \(=\) total positive charge (holes \(+\) ionised donor cores)

and the crystal is neutral. Exactly the same argument with signs reversed holds for p-type: each trivalent acceptor takes an electron to complete its fourth bond, becoming a fixed **negative** acceptor ion, and releases one mobile hole.

The short form: doping does not add charge, it only redistributes it. An arsenic atom is electrically neutral before it enters the lattice, and nothing in the doping process brings charge in from outside — so nothing can make the crystal charged.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: Using Huygen's principle, for a plane wavefront incident on a plane reflecting surface, draw the reflected wavefront. Hence prove laws of reflection.
rows.solution:
**Huygens' principle.** Every point of a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out with the wave's own speed; the new wavefront at a later instant is the surface touching all these wavelets — their common tangent.

**The construction.**

Let MN be the plane reflecting surface, and let a plane wavefront AB travel towards it, meeting it obliquely. A is the end of the wavefront that reaches the surface first; B is the other end, still a distance away.

Draw the incident rays perpendicular to AB, and let the wave speed be \(v\).

While B travels to the surface at C, the wavelet started at A has spread out over the same interval \(t\). So

\(BC = vt \qquad\text{and}\qquad AE = vt\)

where E is on a sphere of radius \(vt\) centred on A. The new wavefront is the tangent from C to that sphere: **EC** is the reflected wavefront, and the reflected rays are drawn perpendicular to it.

Since \(\angle AEC = 90^\circ\) (a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact) and \(\angle ABC = 90^\circ\) (AB is a wavefront, BC a ray), the figure is two right triangles on the same hypotenuse AC.

**Proof of the laws of reflection.**

Compare \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle AEC\):

\(AE = BC = vt\) — the two radii drawn above

\(AC = AC\) — the common hypotenuse

\(\angle ABC = \angle AEC = 90^\circ\)

The triangles are therefore congruent (RHS), so the remaining angles match:

\(\angle BAC = \angle ECA\)

Now identify those angles. The angle of incidence \(i\) is the angle between the incident wavefront AB and the surface — which equals the angle between the incident ray and the normal, since both pairs of lines are mutually perpendicular. That angle is \(\angle BAC\). By the same argument the angle of reflection \(r\) is \(\angle ECA\).

Hence

\(\angle i = \angle r\)

which is the **second law of reflection**.

**The first law** follows from the construction itself: the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the plane of the diagram, which is perpendicular to the reflecting surface. Every wavelet centre and every tangent point used above lies in that one plane, so no part of the construction can carry a ray out of it.

Two features are worth noticing. Nothing in the proof depends on \(v\), so the laws hold for any wave — sound and water waves reflect by the same rule. And because the incident and reflected wavefronts travel in the **same** medium at the same speed, \(AE\) and \(BC\) are necessarily equal; it is precisely this equality that fails at a refracting surface, and that is why refraction bends the ray while reflection does not.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: The de-Broglie wavelength associated with an electron is 0.30 nm. Calculate : (a) the speed, and (b) the kinetic energy (in eV), of the electron.
rows.solution:
**(a) The speed.**

The de Broglie relation ties wavelength to momentum:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = \dfrac{h}{m\lambda}\)

With \(\lambda = 0{\cdot}30\ \mathrm{nm} = 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\), \(h = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\) and \(m = 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}\):

\(v = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31} \times 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-10}} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{2{\cdot}73 \times 10^{-40}}\)

\(v = 2{\cdot}43 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

**(b) The kinetic energy.**

\(K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31} \times (2{\cdot}43 \times 10^{6})^{2}\)

\(K = 2{\cdot}68 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Converting, with \(1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\):

\(K = \dfrac{2{\cdot}68 \times 10^{-18}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 16{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**A cleaner route to (b).** Eliminating \(v\) between the two relations gives the kinetic energy straight from the wavelength:

\(K = \dfrac{h^{2}}{2m\lambda^{2}}\)

Substituting the same numbers returns \(16{\cdot}8\) eV, which is a genuine check rather than a repetition: it never passes through the rounded value of \(v\), so agreement confirms the intermediate step.

The published scheme carries \(v = 2{\cdot}41 \times 10^{6}\) m/s at this point and \(16{\cdot}5\) eV at the end. Dividing \(6{\cdot}63\) by \(2{\cdot}73\) gives \(2{\cdot}4286\), so the intended figures are \(2{\cdot}43 \times 10^{6}\) m/s and \(16{\cdot}8\) eV; the gap is a rounding slip of under two per cent and changes nothing about the method.

**Worth noticing.** An electron of this wavelength is well inside the non-relativistic regime — \(v\) is under one per cent of \(c\) — so \(K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) is safe here. And \(0{\cdot}30\) nm is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is exactly why electrons of a few tens of electronvolts diffract from crystals and why the Davisson-Germer experiment worked at these energies.

rows.stem: For a glass prism of refractive index \(\sqrt{3}\), the value of angle of minimum deviation \(\delta\) is equal to the angle of prism A. Find the angle of prism A. How will the angle \(\delta\) be affected if the prism were immersed in water ?
rows.solution:
**Finding the angle of the prism.**

At minimum deviation the prism formula is

\(\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

The condition given is \(\delta_m = A\), so the numerator becomes \(\sin A\):

\(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\sin A}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

Use the double-angle identity \(\sin A = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\). The sine cancels, which is the whole trick of this question:

\(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{2\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = 2\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)\)

\(\cos\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{A}{2} = 30^\circ\)

\(A = 60^\circ\)

This is the familiar equilateral prism, and with \(\delta_m = A = 60^\circ\) the ray enters at \(i = (A + \delta_m)/2 = 60^\circ\) — a neat special case where the angle of incidence, the prism angle and the minimum deviation are all equal.

**The effect of immersing the prism in water.**

Only the **relative** refractive index enters the prism formula, so what matters is the index of the glass *with respect to its surroundings*:

\(^{w}\mu_g = \dfrac{\mu_g}{\mu_w} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}732}{1{\cdot}33} \approx 1{\cdot}30\)

This is smaller than \(1{\cdot}732\), and since \(\delta_m\) increases with the relative index for a fixed \(A\), **the angle of minimum deviation decreases.**

Putting a number to it, with \(A\) still \(60^\circ\):

\(\sin\left(\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m'}{2}\right) = 1{\cdot}30 \times \sin 30^\circ = 0{\cdot}650\)

\(\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m'}{2} \approx 40{\cdot}6^\circ \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \delta_m' \approx 21^\circ\)

So the deviation falls from \(60^\circ\) to about \(21^\circ\) — a large change, because water removes most of the contrast in optical density that made the glass bend light in the first place.

The limiting case makes the reasoning obvious: were the prism immersed in a liquid of index exactly \(\sqrt{3}\), the relative index would be 1, there would be no refraction at either face, and the deviation would be zero. The prism would simply vanish from view.
